prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit.

We represent: appellant defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a traffic stop becomes unlawful when officers extend it beyond the time reasonably needed without reasonable suspicion.

Cite at least six decisions of the Tenth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**I. The officers unlawfully prolonged the traffic stop beyond the time reasonably needed to complete its mission, because they had no reasonable suspicion of other criminal activity.**

A traffic stop is a seizure under the Fourth Amendment. The Tenth Circuit analyzes it under *Terry v. Ohio*, 392 U.S. 1 (1968). *United States v. Hunnicutt*, 135 F.3d 1345, 1348–49 (10th Cir. 1998). That analysis asks two questions. The first is whether the stop was justified at its inception. The second is whether the officer's actions were reasonably related in scope to the circumstances that justified the stop. *United States v. Mendez*, 118 F.3d 1426, 1429 (10th Cir. 1997); *United States v. West*, 219 F.3d 1171, 1176 (10th Cir. 2000). This appeal concerns the second question.

*A. The stop's authority ends when its mission is, or reasonably should have been, completed.*

The Supreme Court has held that the tolerable duration of a stop "is determined by the seizure's 'mission'": addressing the traffic violation and attending to related safety concerns. *Rodriguez v. United States*, 575 U.S. 348, 354 (2015). Authority for the seizure "ends when tasks tied to the traffic infraction are—or reasonably should have been—completed." *Id.* A stop may not be prolonged for unrelated investigation, even briefly, absent reasonable suspicion. *Id.* at 355–57.

The Tenth Circuit's pre- and post-*Rodriguez* decisions follow the same rule. An officer may request a driver's license and registration, run background checks, and issue a citation or warning. *United States v. Salzano*, 158 F.3d 1107, 1111 (10th Cir. 1998); *United States v. Valenzuela*, 365 F.3d 892, 896–97 (10th Cir. 2004). Once those tasks are done, the driver must be allowed to leave. Further detention is lawful only if the driver consents or the officer has an objectively reasonable and articulable suspicion of illegal activity. *West*, 219 F.3d at 1176; *Salzano*, 158 F.3d at 1111; *United States v. Santos*, 403 F.3d 1120, 1125 (10th Cir. 2005). Unrelated questioning is not independently forbidden. It becomes unlawful when it extends the stop's duration without that justification. *See United States v. Cone*, 868 F.3d 1150, 1153 (10th Cir. 2017); *United States v. Pena-Montes*, 589 F.3d 1048, 1053 (10th Cir. 2009).

*B. The officers extended the stop after its mission was, or should have been, complete.*

[Insert record facts: the time the stop began; when the officer had verified the license, registration, and insurance and run warrant checks; when the citation or warning could have been issued; and what the officer did instead, with record cites.] On this record, the tasks tied to the traffic violation were complete, or reasonably should have been, by [time]. The officers instead kept Appellant on the roadside to [wait for a canine unit / ask unrelated questions / seek consent]. That conduct added [__] minutes to the stop. Under *Rodriguez*, the extension was an unlawful seizure unless it was supported by independent reasonable suspicion.

*C. The government cannot show reasonable suspicion.*

Reasonable suspicion requires "a particularized and objective basis" for suspecting criminal activity, assessed under the totality of the circumstances. *United States v. Karam*, 496 F.3d 1157, 1161–62 (10th Cir. 2007). An officer's "inchoate and unparticularized suspicion or 'hunch'" is not enough. *Terry*, 392 U.S. at 27. This Court has repeatedly held that innocent or ambiguous factors, even in combination, do not justify prolonging a stop. Examples include nervousness, travel on a known highway, an out-of-state or rental vehicle, and an itinerary the officer finds unusual. *Santos*, 403 F.3d at 1126–31; *United States v. Wood*, 106 F.3d 942, 947–48 (10th Cir. 1997); *see also United States v. Bradford*, 423 F.3d 1149, 1157–59 (10th Cir. 2005). The government bears the burden of establishing reasonable suspicion. *Hunnicutt*, 135 F.3d at 1349.

The factors the officers cite here are [nervousness / travel plans / air fresheners / criminal history]. Each is consistent with lawful travel, and none ties Appellant to a particular crime. Taken together, they amount to the kind of hunch that *Santos* and *Wood* found insufficient. Nothing about the stop supplied the particularized suspicion needed to justify detention beyond its mission.

*D. Suppression is required.*

The extended detention was unlawful, and it produced the [contraband / statements] the government seeks to use. Appellant did not give valid consent to continued detention, and any later consent was tainted by the unlawful seizure. *See West*, 219 F.3d at 1178–79. This Court should hold that the stop became unlawful once the officers extended it past its mission. It should reverse the denial of the motion to suppress and vacate the resulting conviction.
